facts.claim: "Skin" is track 8 on Zach Bryan's sixth studio album With Heaven On Top, released January 9, 2026 via Warner Records.
Zach Bryan is the sole songwriter and the producer of "Skin".

Discogs credits on "Skin": Bryan on lead vocals and electric guitar. Jake Weinberg plays bass, drums and acoustic guitar. Chris Braun also plays electric guitar. Read Connolly plays pedal steel. Scott Zhang plays piano. Gabe Wax, Heaven Schmitt and Jake Weinberg sing backing vocals.
"Skin" was engineered by Colton Jean, Gabe Wax, Jake Weinberg and Scott Zhang. It was mixed by Gabe Wax and Jake Weinberg, with Jacob Spitzer assisting. Pete Lyman mastered the album.
The 25-song album was written, recorded and produced by Bryan over several months in Tulsa.
Bryan described the album as songs he and his band recorded across three different houses in Oklahoma over the winter.
"Skin" is widely read as a diss track aimed at Bryan's ex-girlfriend Brianna "Chickenfry" LaPaglia. Bryan has not officially confirmed this.

The lyrics use tattoos as the central image. They include the lines about taking a blade to his own skin and asking "Are you walking 'round Tribeca with him?" Press tied the Tribeca line to LaPaglia, who is based in New York City.
Bryan and LaPaglia had matching "how lucky are we" tattoos. Bryan used the line in his song "28".

With Heaven On Top debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 134,000 album-equivalent units. It was Bryan's second chart-topping album. "Skin" also appears on the companion With Heaven On Top (Acoustic) release.

research.lineage: Oklahoma-based country singer-songwriter storytelling, with confessional breakup material on an album that critics describe as sprawling.

draft:
The question comes first, and it's almost gentle. **"Skin"** opens with Zach Bryan asking "How do tattoos take to your skin?" as if checking on a wound. Then the questions sharpen. Is she walking around Tribeca with someone new? Can she still smell the Wisconsin wind from one late October? By the end of the first verse he's wondering whether she'll make an honest man out of somebody who can't tell a one-night stand from closure, and the tenderness has turned into a jab.

That slide is the song. Bryan wrote and produced it alone, and it's widely read as aimed at his ex, Brianna "Chickenfry" LaPaglia, though he hasn't confirmed it. The context sharpens the central image. The two had matching "how lucky are we" tattoos, a phrase he'd already put in his song "28." So when the chorus has him taking a blade to his old ink and draining the blood between them, it reads less like metaphor than like a plan. "I'm taking a blade to my own skin" is the line that gives him away. The anger in the verses points outward, but the hurt in the chorus lands on his own body. He has to cut himself to get her out.

The second verse is the meanest stretch. Does she love people just to win? Does she still trash her friends? Then he turns it on himself. He's here to take it on the chin, "this time stone-cold sober." There's pride in that, and an admission folded inside it: whatever happened last time, he wasn't steady for it.

The band doesn't dramatize any of this. Bryan cut the album with his group across three houses in Oklahoma over a winter, and the track has that lived-in ease. The groove is slow and relaxed. Acoustic guitar strums, the bass walks underneath, and the drums keep a simple, steady beat. A clean electric guitar holds long notes over the top, and Bryan's slightly raspy voice sits clear in front, with a little reverb on it. Jake Weinberg covers bass, drums and acoustic, and Chris Braun joins Bryan on electric. It's the Oklahoma singer-songwriter mode he's built a career on, kept plain so the words do the cutting.

The refrain swears he'll never touch her again, and it repeats until it stops sounding like a vow and starts sounding like something he's still convincing himself of. The song doesn't close on that promise either. It circles back to the opening questions: the tattoos, Tribeca, that October wind.

It sticks because you hear a man swear he's cutting someone out of his skin while he still can't stop asking how she's doing.
